item.title: Plan for traffic changes: Safety enhancements coming to SR 302 in Gig Harbor
item.description:
Plan for traffic changes: Safety enhancements coming to SR 302 in Gig Harbor leighap@wsdot.wa.gov September 10, 2026 - 9:03am
Date
September 10, 2026 - 12:00pm
Olympic Region
Communications
orfeedback@wsdot.wa.gov
360-357-2600
News summary
GIG HARBOR – From 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 16, and Thursday, Sept. 17, Washington State Department of Transportation crews will begin work to permanently close the right lane of southbound SR 302 between the Purdy Bay Bridge and Burnham Drive Northwest.

Watch for road crews, new configuration near SR 16 interchange

GIG HARBOR – Travelers who drive, walk and roll in Gig Harbor will soon see changes along a portion of State Route 302.

From 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 16, and Thursday, Sept. 17, Washington State Department of Transportation crews will begin work to permanently close the right lane of southbound SR 302 between the Purdy Bay Bridge and Burnham Drive Northwest.

When the work is complete, southbound SR 302 will be reduced to one lane between the Purdy Bridge and Burnham Drive. This is designed to improve safety by reducing opportunities for risky driver behavior including speeding and last-minute merging near the SR 16 interchange.

Other safety enhancements include a new shared use path for walkers and rollers along southbound SR 302 in the shoulder area, and a left turn restriction from Burnham Drive to SR 302. 

The changes were developed after WSDOT traffic and speed studies through the corridor. The recent studies were prompted by citizen and partner agency requests, and an overall increase in all modes of travel on SR 302 between Gig Harbor and the Key Peninsula.

People traveling through the area also can do their part to improve safety by following the speed limit. Risky behaviors, such as speeding and impaired driving, increase the chance of fatal and serious injury crashes.

Travelers are encouraged to sign up for email updates about work on state roads in Pierce County. Real-time travel information is available from the WSDOT app and statewide travel map.

item.description:
WSDOT is updating its Methow Valley State Airport Master Plan creac@wsdot.wa.gov September 10, 2026 - 5:14am
Date
September 10, 2026 - 12:00pm
Christina Crea
communications
christina.crea@wsdot.wa.gov

News summary
WINTHROP – The Washington State Department of Transportation Aviation Division is updating the Methow Valley State Airport Master Plan. The plan will guide airport development and investment through 2046, with particular emphasis on improvements during the next 10 years. The updated plan will identify current and future airport needs, help maintain compliance with Federal Aviation Administration standards and reflect regional priorities.

Learn more about the process and how to get involved during Sept. 24 open house in Winthrop

WINTHROP – The Washington State Department of Transportation Aviation Division is updating the Methow Valley State Airport Master Plan. The plan will guide airport development and investment through 2046, with particular emphasis on improvements during the next 10 years.

The updated plan will identify current and future airport needs, help maintain compliance with Federal Aviation Administration standards and reflect regional priorities.

Community members, airport users, neighbors and other interested parties are invited to learn about the master plan update and share their perspectives during a hybrid public open house on Thursday, Sept. 24. The meeting will be held in person at The Winthrop Barn Auditorium and online through Zoom. 

Methow Valley State Airport Master Plan open house information

When:  5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 24

Where:  Main Hall at The Winthrop Barn Auditorium, 51 State Route 20, Winthrop

Details:  For those attending online via Zoom: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/87947749934?pwd=S5Aa9z5m9rBVFRclmMPl1kKbDujyAG.1

Free language assistance and accommodations for people with disabilities are available upon request. Requests can be made by emailing christina.crea@wsdot.wa.gov by Sept. 14.

The meeting will begin with a presentation about the master planning process and the role of the project’s Technical Advisory Group, or TAG. The TAG includes representatives from the local aviation community, emergency services, private aviation interests and neighborhoods surrounding the airport.

TAG members will take part in a facilitated discussion about the challenges and opportunities with current and future airport uses. People attending online will be able to view the presentation and participate remotely.

The second part of the meeting will be an in-person open house. Community members can speak with the project team and review information about:

  • The master planning process and project milestones.
  • Existing airport facilities and features.
  • Current and potential aviation trends.
  • Anticipated airport needs over the next 20 years with an emphasis on the next 10 years.
  • Upcoming opportunities for public involvement.

The master plan update will examine several aspects of the airport, including:

  • Runway, taxiway and apron facilities.
  • Airport access, hangar areas and utilities.
  • Airport signage, fencing, gates and security.
  • Helicopter, glider and seasonal operational needs.
  • Compatibility with U.S. Forest Service smokejumper operations.
  • Emergency response and wildland firefighting needs.
  • Advanced air mobility opportunities.
  • Environmental considerations and surrounding land uses.
  • Future projects, costs, funding opportunities and implementation priorities.

Public input will help WSDOT and the project team better understand how the airport serves the region today and what should be considered as the master plan is developed. Feedback received during this first phase will help identify how airport users view current operations, the quality of existing facilities and future needs based on projected trends and expected use.

Two more public meetings are anticipated later in the planning process and will be virtual only. The second meeting will focus on potential alternatives for updating airport facilities to meet future demands and needs. The third meeting will present the preferred alternative or most promising solutions and/or upgrades. It will also include the Capital Improvement Plan, a document that highlights the funding and implementation and construction capabilities and timeline.

People who cannot attend the Sept. 24 open house can learn more and provide feedback at https://engage.wsdot.wa.gov/methow-valley-airport.

Free internet access

Free, temporary internet access may be available to those who do not have broadband services. Washington state’s open data portal has created a map of public libraries offering drive up Wi-Fi, including locations, hours and contact information.

item.title: Opening Sept. 13: First section of SR 167 Expressway in north Pierce County
item.description:
Opening Sept. 13: First section of SR 167 Expressway in north Pierce County OlsenK@wsdot.wa.gov September 8, 2026 - 11:07am
Date
September 8, 2026 - 12:00pm
Kris Olsen
communications
kris.olsen@wsdot.wa.gov
206-440-4704
Road
SR 167
News summary
FIFE – A highly anticipated new section of State Route 167 in north Pierce County is just days away from opening. The Washington State Department of Transportation will open the first 2-mile segment of the SR 167 Expressway between Interstate 5 in Fife and SR 509 near the Port of Tacoma by 9 a.m. Sunday, Sept. 13.

People can choose a more direct route between I-5 in Fife and the Port of Tacoma 

FIFE – A highly anticipated new section of State Route 167 in north Pierce County is just days away from opening. The Washington State Department of Transportation will open the first 2-mile segment of the SR 167 Expressway between Interstate 5 in Fife and SR 509 near the Port of Tacoma by 9 a.m. Sunday, Sept. 13.

The SR 167 Completion Project is part of WSDOT’s $2.83 billion Puget Sound Gateway Program. Crews on the SR 167 project are building a total of 6 miles of new highway between SR 410 near Puyallup and SR 509 in Tacoma, on Puyallup Tribe of Indians land.

“Our people have lived and worked on this land since time immemorial,” said Puyallup Tribe Chairman Bill Sterud. “Completing SR 167 brings new opportunities that will contribute to the ongoing success of our tribe and continued economic vitality for the region. I want to especially thank WSDOT for working with our team to restore more than 165 acres of wetlands as part of this project.”

“We wouldn’t be opening this new highway in 2026 without the collaboration of the Puyallup Tribe and 17 other jurisdictions,” said House Transportation Committee Chairman Jake Fey. “All of our partners provided valuable guidance, planning support and $140 million in contributions of cash, land and local grants to the Gateway program. This is an investment in our future. The completion of this segment to the Port of Tacoma has been a priority that has been in planning for over 20 years. It’s great that this economic development project is now being realized which substantially enhances the competitiveness of the Port of Tacoma.”

Critical new connection for freight

The first 2 miles of the expressway fills a critical gap in the state’s highway network, giving freight haulers a more reliable and faster trip.

“More efficient connections benefit our region, the state and the nation,” said Port of Tacoma Commission President Dick Marzano. “The Port of Tacoma’s lines of business, combined with cargo operations in Tacoma managed by The Northwest Seaport Alliance, support more than 41,000 jobs and generate more than $100 million in state tax revenue. A vibrant port is critical to helping our region thrive and grown family-wage jobs.”

The new route will be open to all vehicles and is expected to help relieve congestion on local streets near the port.

The first 2 miles

The first segment of the new expressway features two lanes in each direction between I-5 and 54th Avenue East.

  • Southbound I-5 drivers can enter the expressway near the Fife curve and exit at 54th Avenue East or southbound SR 509.
  • Drivers can enter the expressway from northbound SR 509 near the Port of Tacoma or a new roundabout on 54th Avenue East.
  • All northbound travelers must exit to northbound I-5 until the final construction stages are complete.

This stage of the SR 167 Completion Project includes:

  • A new bridge over I-5 with the world’s second longest precast concrete girders.
  • Two new bridges on I-5 for Hylebos Creek to flow under.
  • 17 additional bridges and structures.
  • A new intersection at SR 509 and Alexander Avenue East.

“Completing SR 167 is an investment in the people who live and work in this area,” said Puget Sound Gateway Program Administrator Ricky Bhalla. “When people can reliably access jobs and communities are connected, our entire region succeeds.”

Tolling begins in December

The new expressway will be tolled beginning in December. Drivers with a Good To Go!  pass will be charged $1 in each direction for the section west of I-5. Vehicles with three or more axles will be charged higher toll rates.

The Washington State Transportation Commission adopted the toll rate for SR 167 on June 17, 2025. Toll funding will help pay for construction and ongoing maintenance.

Wetland and creek restoration program

As part of the project, crews also restored more than 165 acres of wetlands west and east of the I-5 Fife curve. The original wetlands were repurposed for agricultural and industrial use decades ago. WSDOT worked closely with the Puyallup Tribe of Indians on a first-of-its-kind effort to return the area to its natural state.

Crews built new channels for Hylebos Creek and the Surprise Lake tributary. They also planted more than 300,000 native species of shrubs and trees. The restoration allows the area to act as a floodplain again, reducing the risk of chronic I-5 flooding during heavy storms while improving habitat and providing long-term benefits to fish and wildlife.

The next stages of expressway construction

Crews are currently working on additional construction stages that will:

  • Widen an existing section of SR 167 between SR 410 near Puyallup to North Meridian Avenue.
  • Build another 4 miles of new highway between North Meridian Avenue and I-5 where it will connect with the section opening Sept. 13.
  • Complete the spuyaləpabš Trail, a shared-use path that features artwork by Coast Salish artists.

The remaining 4 miles are scheduled to open to traffic in June 2029.

Photos of construction work and a 3D video tour are available online.

Puget Sound Gateway Program

In addition to the SR 167 Completion Project, the Puget Sound Gateway Program also includes the SR 509 Completion Project in south King County. Together, the two projects complete critical missing links in Washington’s highway and freight network.

item.title: First of two weekend-long closures of I-5 express lanes in Seattle planned for Sept. 11-14
item.description:
First of two weekend-long closures of I-5 express lanes in Seattle planned for Sept. 11-14 pearcet@wsdot.wa.gov September 3, 2026 - 12:47pm
Date
September 3, 2026 - 12:00pm
Tom Pearce
communications
tom.pearce@wsdot.wa.gov
206-492-9555
News summary
SEATTLE – People traveling to, through and around Seattle should plan for two upcoming weekend-long closures of the Interstate 5 express lanes, Sept. 11-14 and Oct. 2-5.

SEATTLE – People traveling to, through and around Seattle should plan for two upcoming weekend-long closures of the Interstate 5 express lanes. Crews working on the Revive I-5: Ship Canal Bridge Preservation project will use the closures to access the underside of the bridge for drainage improvements.

The I-5 express lanes have only been open northbound during construction. The Washington State Department of Transportation has scheduled two weekend-long full closures of the express lanes for this work:

  • 11 p.m. Friday, Sept. 11, to 5 a.m. Monday, Sept. 14.
  • 11 p.m. Friday, Oct. 2, to 5 a.m. Monday, Oct. 5.

Most of the drainage work crews have been working on in 2026 is on the underside of the bridge and has been completed using scaffolding installed in 2024. Since not all sections are accessible via scaffolding, closures of the express lanes are needed to complete the work in this area. Crews will connect drains installed during an earlier phase of the project to the permanent drainage system. Drainage work will resume in 2027 when construction shifts to the southbound lanes of I-5.

Crews need to complete this work before the fall rains arrive. Planning the express lane closures for two weekends provides crews the uninterrupted time they need to get the work done.

Project benefits

Completing these connections will help move water off the bridge more effectively. This supports safer driving conditions by reducing standing water on the roadway and helps protect the new concrete bridge deck from water-related deterioration.

Plan ahead

People should expect increased congestion and longer travel times through the downtown Seattle corridor during the two weekend closures. Higher traffic volumes are also expected on other north-south routes as people traveling look for alternate routes and modes. There is no single alternate route that can absorb I-5 traffic, which makes planning ahead and allowing additional travel time especially important, so travelers should check resources like WSDOT’s online Travel Center map and the WSDOT mobile app before leaving.

item.title: Long weekend and overnight closures on the horizon for US 101 Hoh River Bridge south of Forks
item.description:
Long weekend and overnight closures on the horizon for US 101 Hoh River Bridge south of Forks krulism@wsdot.wa.gov September 2, 2026 - 1:13pm
Date
September 2, 2026 - 12:00pm
Olympic Region
communications
orfeedback@wsdot.wa.gov
360-357-2600
Road
US 101
News summary
FORKS – Travelers who use US 101 between Forks and Hoquiam on the west side of the Olympic Peninsula will need to prepare for hours-long detours during overnight and around-the-clock closures at the US 101 Hoh River Bridge.

Only detour is via US 101 along Hood Canal while crews repair the 95-year-old bridge

FORKS – Travelers who use US 101 between Forks and Hoquiam on the west side of the Olympic Peninsula will need to prepare for hours-long detours during overnight and around-the-clock closures at the US 101 Hoh River Bridge.

Starting Monday, Sept. 14, the Washington State Department of Transportation’s emergency contractor, Hamilton Construction, will bring in equipment needed to replace four floor beams at two joints under the bridge deck.

From Monday, Sept. 14 to Tuesday, Sept. 22, each night from 10:30 p.m. to 5:30 a.m., the US 101 Hoh River Bridge will close to all traffic. During the overnight closures, crews will install a work deck and containment system on the bridge that is needed to perform the repairs.

Extended weekend closures for three weekends

Once the scaffolding is in place, crews will close the bridge to traffic for up to six days in a row for three weeks to make the repairs. The 95-year-old bridge is not wide enough to create a work zone and keep one travel lane open. The closures are scheduled for the following dates:

  • 5 a.m. Thursday, Sept. 24 to 5 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 29
  • 5 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 1 to noon Tuesday, Oct. 6
  • 5 a.m. Thursday Oct. 8 to noon Tuesday, Oct. 13

After each six-day closure, the bridge will be inspected prior to reopening to single-lane alternating traffic.

Emergency responders will have pedestrian access across the bridge during the work, provided by the contractor. The pedestrian access is not open to the public.

Long detour during closures

There is no alternative route or detour available across the Hoh River. Travelers heading between Forks and Hoquiam will need to take US 101 along Hood Canal – a four-hour trip. Likewise, visitors at Olympic National Park’s Hurricane Ridge or Lake Crescent wanting to visit Kalaloch, Ruby Beach or Lake Quinault will need to take US 101 along Hood Canal to SR 108, SR 8, US 12 and back to US 101.

Olympic National Park visitors are strongly encouraged to plan ahead and utilize the park’s travel time maps.

Why repairs are needed

Earlier this summer, state bridge engineers found cracks in support beams and the steel that support the driving surface on the 95-year-old bridge. On July 14, one-way alternating traffic and a speed limit reduction of 25 mph was put in place across the bridge. Traffic on US 101 is controlled by temporary traffic lights on either side of the bridge.

The repairs taking place in September and October will keep the bridge open until a long-term extensive repair can be implemented to restore load carrying capacity of the bridge. A single lane of travel across the bridge will remain in place until a permanent repair can be made.

About the bridge

Located at milepost 176.5 on US 101, the 494.5-foot-long bridge spans the Hoh River. The bridge carries an average of 1,400 vehicles across it each day. Oversized loads have been restricted on the bridge since 2010. This bridge was built in 1931. It is one of 342 bridges in WSDOT’s current inventory that is over 80 years old.

Whenever near work zones please:

  • Slow down – drive the posted speeds, they're there for everyone’s safety.
  • Be kind – workers are out there helping to keep everyone safe and improve the roadways.
  • Pay attention – both to workers directing traffic and to fellow travelers.
  • Stay calm – expect delays, leave early or take alternate routes if possible.

Traveler resources

Travelers are encouraged to visit the WSDOT online open house for details on projects happening around the Olympic Peninsula. Sign up for email updates about work on state highways in Jefferson and Clallam counties. Real-time travel information is available on the WSDOT app and statewide travel map.

item.title: Record summer for Washington State Ferries culminates with busy Labor Day weekend
item.description:
Record summer for Washington State Ferries culminates with busy Labor Day weekend fujiokj@wsdot.wa.gov September 1, 2026 - 7:52am
Date
September 1, 2026 - 12:00pm
Dana Warr
communications
Dana.Warr@wsdot.wa.gov
206-719-6819
WSF media hotline
communications
WSFComms@wsdot.wa.gov
206-402-8070
News summary
SEATTLE – The final tsunami of summer travelers is heading for Washington State Ferries. Close to 400,000 people are expected on board between Thursday, Sept. 3, and Monday, Sept. 7.

Nearly 400,000 riders to set sail on holiday trips

SEATTLE – The final tsunami of summer travelers is heading for Washington State Ferries. Close to 400,000 people are expected on board between Thursday, Sept. 3, and Monday, Sept. 7.

The Labor Day travel rush will cap WSF’s busiest summer since 2019. From Memorial Day through the final Sunday in August, ridership has totaled nearly 7 million. That’s an increase of nearly 100,000 over the same period in 2025.

Plan ahead for Labor Day ferry travel 

People boarding a vessel in a vehicle should use the Washington State Department of Transportation mobile app or visit the WSF website before heading to the terminal. Both feature sailing schedules, live terminal conditions, rider alerts, a real-time map and vehicle reservations.

Saturday, Sept. 5, is expected to see the heaviest passenger traffic. So far in 2026, WSF has recorded six days with more than 90,000 riders. All six were Saturdays, including:

  • 99,557 on Aug. 8 (busiest day since Aug. 17, 2019).
  • 98,174 on July 18.
  • 96,243 on Aug. 15.
  • 93,667 on July 25.
  • 93,329 on Aug. 1.
  • 93,067 on July 3.

“Seeing more people ride with us is a clear sign that we’re moving in the right direction and rebuilding confidence in our system,” said Steve Nevey, head of WSF. “We’re not taking that for granted. We remain focused on recruiting, training and retaining the employees we need to deliver reliable service. At the same time, we’re working to improve on-time performance, and our crews and maintenance teams are doing all they can to keep our aging fleet sailing safely until our new ferries arrive.”

Busy travel times

The busiest sailings for vehicles will likely be westbound (or onto an island) Thursday and Friday, Sept. 3-4, then eastbound (or off island) Sunday and Monday, Sept. 6-7. Prepare for long lines and extended wait times. To reduce or eliminate waiting, riders should consider taking early-morning or late-night sailings or using transit to walk or bike onto the ferry if possible.

Holiday schedules

On Labor Day, Sept. 7, there will be a few holiday adjustments to daily schedules for the Anacortes/San Juan Islands, Edmonds/Kingston, Port Townsend/Coupeville and Point Defiance/Tahlequah routes. These changes are marked online on each schedule by route. Seattle/Bainbridge and Fauntleroy/Vashon/Southworth will run on their weekend/holiday timetables.

People using state highways to get to the ferry terminal should plan for potential holiday travel backups and delays by checking real-time traffic information on the WSDOT mobile app or online using the WSDOT travel map feature.

WSF, a division of WSDOT, is the largest ferry system in the U.S. and safely and efficiently carries tens of millions of people a year through some of the most majestic scenery in the world.

item.title: New SR 14 connection in Bingen puts train delays in the rearview mirror
item.description:
New SR 14 connection in Bingen puts train delays in the rearview mirror hannons@wsdot.wa.gov August 27, 2026 - 3:21pm
Date
August 27, 2026 - 12:00pm
Sarah Hannon-Nein
Communications Manager
sarah.hannon-nein@wsdot.wa.gov
360-989-7589
News summary
BINGEN – Travelers in Bingen now have a safer, more reliable connection between State Route 14, Bingen Point and the Port of Klickitat, without having to stop and wait for passing trains. On Thursday, Aug. 27, the Washington State Department of Transportation joined the city of Bingen, Port of Klickitat, BNSF Railway and elected officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony celebrating the functional completion of the SR 14 Bingen Access Improvements project.

Ribbon cutting celebrates new underpass and roundabout improving access to Bingen Point and the Port of Klickitat

BINGEN – Travelers in Bingen now have a safer, more reliable connection between State Route 14, Bingen Point and the Port of Klickitat, without having to stop and wait for passing trains.

On Thursday, Aug. 27, the Washington State Department of Transportation joined the city of Bingen, Port of Klickitat, BNSF Railway and elected officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony celebrating the functional completion of the SR 14 Bingen Access Improvements project.

The event marked the end of nearly 12 years of planning and coordination and one year of construction. The $34.3 million project built a new road beneath the BNSF tracks and a roundabout at SR 14 and Elm Street, creating a new connection between the highway, Bingen Point and the Port of Klickitat.

Previously, travelers heading between SR 14 and Bingen Point had to cross the railroad tracks. When trains passed through, they could block the crossing for several minutes, delaying travelers, freight and emergency responders while traffic backed up onto SR 14. The new underpass separates road and rail traffic, allowing both to keep moving.

“For years, people had to wait for trains to pass before they could get to Bingen Point,” said WSDOT Southwest Region Project Engineer TJ Prendergast. “Now, travelers and freight can keep moving and emergency responders have a direct way in when every second matters.”

The new Juniper Street now travels underneath the railroad tracks, connecting SR 14 and Steuben Street with Bingen Point and the Port of Klickitat.

The project also built a new roundabout at SR 14 and Elm Street to improve safety and keep traffic moving through the intersection. At the center of the roundabout is a historic pond boat, used to move logs near mills, honoring the region's timber heritage.

Bringing the project from planning to completion took years of coordination and community support. WSDOT contractor Kerr Contractors completed the roadway improvements, including Juniper Street, the underpass and the new roundabout. Together, these improvements create a safer, more reliable connection that will keep people and goods moving through Bingen for years to come.

item.title: Ready, set, road trip: WSDOT offers Labor Day weekend travel tools and tips
item.description:
Ready, set, road trip: WSDOT offers Labor Day weekend travel tools and tips wernerc@wsdot.wa.gov August 24, 2026 - 7:58am
Date
August 24, 2026 - 12:00pm
Tina Werner
Communications
christina.werner@wsdot.wa.gov
360-867-8754
News summary
OLYMPIA – Labor Day weekend will bring lots of travel and congestion to state highways, waterways, at state airports and along pedestrian trails.

Plan ahead for holiday weekend congestion Sept. 4-7

OLYMPIA – Labor Day weekend will bring lots of travel and congestion to state highways, waterways, at state airports and along pedestrian trails.

The Washington State Department of Transportation urges travelers to plan ahead, stay alert and give themselves extra time to get to their destinations. WSDOT has Labor Day weekend travel charts to help people beat the rush as well as other tools and tips to make all types of travel easier.

The charts highlight the best and worst times to travel on key state highways most prone to holiday congestion, including:

  • US 2 between Skykomish and Stevens Pass
  • Interstate 90 between North Bend and Cle Elum
  • I-5 between Lacey and Tacoma
  • I-5 between Bellingham and the Canadian border

Whether traveling across town or across the state, WSDOT encourages travelers to “know before you go” by following these tips:

  • Get informed about WSDOT's online tools, including the WSDOT mobile app, traffic cameras and email alerts.
  • Visit online traveler information for traffic, weather, ferry schedules and a real-time travel map.
  • Follow WSDOT on social media including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Bluesky and X.
  • Identify potential safety rest areas before heading out, to ensure enough breaks to avoid drowsy driving.
  • Have a backup outdoor destination in mind, as parks and other outdoor recreation sites tend to fill up quickly on holiday weekends. If a site’s parking lot is full, never park along road shoulders – this is unsafe for everyone on the roadway, including emergency responders.

Most highway construction paused

Most highway construction will pause to help ease congestion starting Friday, Sept. 4, but delays are still likely – especially in popular areas or due to crashes or wildfires. The Revive I-5 work zone over the Ship Canal Bridge remains in place.

Stay alert to fire danger

Fire danger remains high across the state. If traveling near active wildfires, stay alert and up to date on closures as winds can shift quickly. These tips can help prevent roadside fires:

  • Never throw a lit cigarette or any other flammable material out of vehicle windows. 
  • Keep towing chains from dragging on pavement to avoid sparks.
  • Do not park on dry grass, the heat from exhaust systems can spark a brush fire.
  • If a brush fire is spotted with no emergency crews around, be sure to alert authorities – do not assume someone else has called it in.
  • Always call 911 for real-time emergencies, as opposed to notifying WSDOT or the Washington State Patrol via social media or email.

Ferry travel

Washington State Ferry routes also are expected to be busy. Reservations are strongly encouraged on routes that offer them. People boarding a ferry by vehicle can likely expect the busiest sailings and longer wait times to be westbound (or onto an island) Thursday and Friday, Sept. 3-4 and eastbound (or departing an island) Sunday and Monday, Sept. 6-7. Walk-on passengers can bypass vehicle lines and usually board much faster. Other helpful tips to consider:

  • All riders should double-check the sailing schedules and sign up to receive rider alerts for service updates.
  • Visit Washington State Ferries for details on vehicle reservations for some routes, tracking ferries on a real-time map and checking terminal status.
  • State Route 160/Sedgwick Road between SR 16 and the Southworth Ferry Terminal remains closed through October for a fish barrier correction project at Salmonberry Creek. A signed detour is in place for vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians.

Vantage Bridge

To help accommodate increased travel during the holiday weekend, all lanes of I-90 across the Vantage Bridge will be open Friday, Sept. 4, through Monday, Sept. 7. Beginning Tuesday, Sept. 8, the bridge will return to one lane in each direction around the clock through Monday, Nov. 2, when construction pauses for winter. This project is part of a long-term effort to replace the deteriorating bridge deck and is expected to be complete by fall 2028.

Tolling

In the Puget Sound region, weekend toll rates will be in effect beginning Monday, Sept. 7 on the SR 520 bridge, SR 99 tunnel and SR 509 Expressway. The I-405 and SR 167 express toll lanes will be free and open to all drivers Monday, Sept. 7. Out-of-town travelers, including those using rental cars, can learn about toll roads and temporary account payment options on the Good To Go! visitors page.

Trains, airports and transit

Travelers making a trip by train, personal aircraft or bus also should plan ahead to avoid holiday delays:

  • Amtrak Cascades passengers are encouraged to purchase tickets early and plan to arrive at the station at least one hour before departure. Trains run between Vancouver, British Columbia and Eugene, Oregon, stopping at 18 stations along the way. Buses also are available for travel between Seattle and Vancouver, British Columbia and between Seattle and Bellingham. Visit www.AmtrakCascades.com or call 800-USA-RAIL for tickets and schedules.
  • For information about traveling via state-sponsored airports, visit WSDOT’s airport list or call 360-618-2477.
  • Check with local public transit agencies for any holiday schedule or service changes, including some Dial-A-Ride and fixed-route service that may not run on holidays.

News summary
ENUMCLAW – New system adds another tool to help prevent damaging bridge strikes

ENUMCLAW – A new over height vehicle detection system is now in place on the State Route 410 White River Bridge, giving drivers of taller vehicles another clear warning before they reach the bridge connecting the communities of Enumclaw and Buckley. 

Contractor crews working for the Washington State Department of Transportation installed the new system recently following the August 2025 bridge strike that caused significant damage to the bridge and led to an extended closure. Crews worked seven days a week to repair the structure and reopen the bridge. Theat closure affected thousands of people who rely on the bridge each day, including commuters, freight and businesses located in these communities.

The new system uses sensors to detect vehicles that may be too tall to safely cross under the bridge. When an over height vehicle is detected, the system will activate warning signs, flashing beacons and audible alarms to alert the driver before they reach the bridge.

"This bridge is a critical connection for communities on both sides of the White River," said Governor Bob Ferguson. "We're giving it another layer of protection for travelers, and for the people who depend on this route every day." 

A tool to help prevent future bridge strikes

The new over height detection system does not change the 14-foot bridge clearance and does not replace the responsibility drivers have to know the height of their vehicle and load and obtain any required permits for travel. 

Drivers of tall vehicles should:

  • Know the height of their vehicle, equipment and load before traveling and obtain an oversize vehicle permit if applicable.
  • Use WSDOT's online vertical clearance trip planner to identify bridge clearances along planned routes.
  • Check route restrictions before using SR 410.
  • Obey all posted bridge clearance signs.
  • Stop if the over height warning system activates.
  • Use approved alternate routes when required. 

Bridge strikes are preventable, but their impacts can be significant. A single over height vehicle can damage a bridge, close a highway and disrupt travel for an entire region.

"This is about prevention," said Secretary of Transportation Julie Meredith. "We need drivers to do their part, and this system gives them one more opportunity to make the safe choice before a bridge strike happens."

In the 2026 Supplemental Transportation Budget, the Legislature also directed WSDOT to analyze recent bridge strikes in Washington. WSDOT is asked to recommend ways to reduce future strikes, including potential improvements to physical infrastructure, posted warning signs and additional driver information. A report is due to the Legislature in September 2026.

Bridge background

The White River Bridge is a steel truss bridge built in 1949. It carries an average of 22,099 vehicles each day. WSDOT bridges are inspected on a two-year cycle. The last inspection of this bridge took place in April 2025, and the bridge was determined to be in fair condition. A bridge is expected to have a service life of 80 years based on current standards. The average age of a state-owned vehicular bridge is 51 years.

Real time travel information is available from WSDOT’s online Travel Center map, the WSDOT mobile app and by signing up for WSDOT’s email updates.

OAK HARBOR – Island County travelers soon will see a permanent speed limit decrease along nearly 2 miles of State Route 20 through and north of Oak Harbor.

OAK HARBOR – Island County travelers soon will see a permanent speed limit decrease along nearly 2 miles of State Route 20 through and north of Oak Harbor.

The speed limit will be reduced from 50 and 55 mph to 45 mph along both directions of SR 20 near the new roundabout at West Fakkema Road between mileposts 33.69 and 35.06. The decision to reduce the speed limit was made in response to a review of new speed data after the installation of the new West Fakkema Road roundabout and in coordination with Oak Harbor Public Works officials.

Washington State Department of Transportation maintenance crews will replace the existing speed limit signs with new signs the week of Monday, Aug. 24. The new 45 mph speed limit is enforceable as soon as the signs are installed.

People traveling through the area can do their part to improve safety by following the speed limit, obeying posted signs and staying focused and sober while driving.
